text.p: These are the leading stories in the Pakistani press on Friday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
THE NEWS
- Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan said India was sending mixed signals about the foreign secretary level talks between India and Pakistan.

- Opposition leader Benazir Bhutto condemned as un-Islamic the raid of a law enforcing agency on the residence of a woman member of the National Assembly Fahmida Mirza, who belongs to her Pakistan People's Party.
- The government has allowed all petroleum exploration and production companies duty-free import of machinery and equipment which are not manufactured locally.
THE MUSLIM
- British Minister of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs Derek Fatchett is to pay a four-day visit to Pakistan.
THE FRONTIER POST
- Pakistan and South Africa signed two letters of intent for enhancing cooperation.
DAWN
- Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub said recent Indian actions would not contribute to improving relations, but would heighten tension and cloud the peace process.

- Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif described the firing near Sialkot which killed a Pakistani paramilitary officer as an act of aggression by India, saying it was deplorable when the two countries were preparing for talks.
- One person was shot dead and six vehicles were set ablaze in Karachi, while the police arrested 19 workers of the Haqiqi splinter faction of the ethnic Mohajir National Movement (MQM).

- The budget for 1997/98 (July-June) to be presented in the National Assembly on Friday is expected to show a deficit of 30 billion rupees to be covereed by tax adjustments worth 10 billion and cuts in unproductive expenditure worth 20 billion.
- A gang of five gunmen kidnapped Pir Mazharul Haq, deputy opposition leader in the Sindh provincial assembly.
- Two more people fell victim to sectarian squabbles in the city of Faisalabad, in Punjab province, bringing the death toll to 15 in three months.

- A five-member full bench of the House of Lords (supreme Court) in London unanimously allowed two Pakistan-born employees of the collapsed Bank of Credit and Commerce International to claim stigma compensation from the bank liquidators.
- Pakistan plans to convene a conference of five countries -- Iran, Pakistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan -- to discuss ways to end the internecine fighting in Afghanistan.

- A UAE-based consortium led by Sheikh Nahayan bin Mubarak al-Nahayan offered 39 rupees per share for Habib Credit and Exchange Bank, which the Privatisation Commission accepted and submitted to a cabinet committee for final approval.
- Foreign exchange reserves of Pakistan declined slightly to $1.064 billion on June 7 from $1.074 on May 31.
- Korea's Daewoo Corporation is considering setting up a holding company in Pakistan which invest in various projects.
BUSINESS RECORDER
- The government may resume the Afghan transit trade facility and lift its ban on 23 items, following Iran's action in stopping all Afghan-bound cargo via Bandar Abbas from June 7.

- Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz will present the 1997/98 budget with an outlay of over 550 billion rupees, the main thrust of which will be to fortify the government's economic revival packages and conform to IMF criteria for successful ESAF negotiations.
- The Corporate Law Authroity has asked the Karachi Stock Exchange to restructure its board of directors and appoint at least 33 percent of them from non-broker/members community.
-- Islamabad newsroom 274757
